---
title: "Loss Curve"
---

The loss curve is the single most-watched plot in deep learning, and reading it well is a genuine skill. Let me build the concept up properly.

## What the curve actually plots

The y-axis is the **loss value** (averaged over a dataset), the x-axis is **training progress** (epochs — one full pass over the training data). You plot it for *two* datasets at once:

```
loss
  │ ●  ← training loss: computed on data the
  │  ●    model learns from. Gradient descent
  │   ●   is literally pushing THIS down.
  │    ●●●●●●●●●
  │
  │ ○  ← validation loss: computed on held-out
  │  ○○   data the model NEVER updates weights on.
  │     ○○○○○○○   This is the HONEST signal.
  └──────────────────────► epochs
```

The crucial asymmetry: training loss almost always falls, because the model is directly minimizing it. Validation loss is the one that tells you the truth — whether what the model learned actually *generalizes* to data it hasn't seen.

## Why the gap is the whole story

A model can lower its training loss in two fundamentally different ways:

```
  Learn REAL patterns  ──→ helps on training AND validation
  Memorize NOISE/quirks ──→ helps on training, USELESS (then harmful) on validation
   specific to the
   training set
```

The gap between the two curves separates these two behaviors. A small, stable gap means the model is learning structure that transfers. A *growing* gap means the model is increasingly just memorizing its training data.

## The three canonical shapes

**Underfitting** — both curves high, close together, flat or barely moving:

```
loss
  │●○●○●○●○●○●○   both stuck high, riding together
  │
  └──────────────► epochs
```
The model hasn't even captured the training signal. Causes: too little capacity, too few epochs, learning rate too low. The model is too simple for the problem.

**Good fit** — both descend and settle low, with a modest stable gap:

```
loss
  │●
  │ ○
  │  ●○
  │    ●●○○
  │       ●●●●●●  ← train
  │        ○○○○○  ← val, small steady gap above
  └──────────────► epochs
```

**Overfitting** — train keeps falling toward zero, but val descends, bottoms out, then *turns upward*:

```
loss
  │○            ○○○  ← val turns back UP
  │ ●○        ○○
  │   ●○    ○○        ← the divergence point
  │     ●○○○            is the key event
  │       ●●●●●●●●●●  ← train keeps sliding toward 0
  └──────────────────► epochs
         ▲
    val minimum
```
This U-shape in the validation curve, while training keeps dropping, is the signature of overfitting. The model is now memorizing training-set noise — which lowers train loss but actively hurts on unseen data.

## Early stopping = pick the val minimum

Once you see the shape above, the best model isn't the one at the end of training — it's the snapshot at the **validation minimum**. Everything to the left is still improving; everything to the right is memorizing.

```
        keep training              stop here
        (still improving)      (val starts rising)
   ─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────
                             ▲
                      best generalization
```

Conceptually, early stopping watches validation loss and halts when it stops improving — usually with a **patience** parameter (e.g. "stop if no improvement for 10 epochs"), because the curve is noisy and you don't want to react to a single bad epoch. You then restore the weights from the best epoch, not the last one.

## Two subtleties that confuse newcomers

**Validation loss can sit *below* training loss early on.** This looks alarming but is often normal — regularization like dropout is active during training but switched off during validation, so the model is "handicapped" while you measure train loss. Not a bug.

**Validation *loss* can rise while a *metric* like accuracy holds steady.** This ties straight back to our loss-vs-metric distinction. Loss heavily penalizes *confident wrong answers*. A model can grow overconfident — pushing loss up — while still putting predictions on the correct side of the decision boundary, so accuracy stays flat. This is why "which quantity do I early-stop on?" is a real decision, not an obvious one. For something like tumor classification you might stop on the metric you actually report, not on raw loss.

---

So the mental model: **train loss is what's optimized, validation loss is what's trusted, and the relationship between the two curves — together, not individually — is the diagnostic instrument.**
